name_en: Liu Bao Forms and Grades (Baskets, Bricks, Lao Cha Po)
cultivar: Cangwu and Liubao population bushes and Guangxi large-leaf cultivars
processing: The same post-fermented Liu Bao leaf (fixed, rolled, piled, dried, steamed) finished in different ways: lightly packed into large or small bamboo baskets, or pressed into bricks, cakes or small tuo. Lao Cha Po is different: mature autumn and winter leaves, traditionally blanched in water and more recently steamed, then dried and stored.
harvest_season: Grades Te Ji to 6 are sorted by the tenderness of the leaf; Lao Cha Po is picked in autumn and winter from current-year or older mature leaves, with leaf from around and after Frost's Descent in late October most prized.
appearance_dry: Ranges from fine, even dark leaf in the top grades to stemmy coarse leaf in grade 5–6 and the large, papery, yellow-brown whole leaves of Lao Cha Po.
appearance_liquor: Red-amber for graded leaf; Lao Cha Po brews a clear golden-orange.
appearance_wet: Dark reddish-brown for graded tea; Lao Cha Po shows big, thin, intact old leaves.
taste_profile: Graded Liu Bao runs from smooth and refined (Te Ji) to rustic and sweet (grade 5–6); Lao Cha Po is light, honeyed and grain-like with a faint medicinal note and almost no bitterness.

brewing.notes: Graded leaf: two rinses then short steeps with boiling water. Lao Cha Po and coarse grades are best simmered: a handful per litre for 5–10 minutes, served all day.

vintage_note: All forms are sold by pressing or packing year: big baskets and bricks from the Wuzhou factories carry year and batch numbers and sit on the market at 2–20 years, small retail baskets are usually 3–10 years, and Lao Cha Po is sold at anything from 5 to 20 years because its coarse leaf changes slowly. Farmhouse (nong jia) lots are dated by the farmer's word.
description:
Liu Bao is one tea sold in many shapes, and knowing the shapes saves money. The traditional unit is the big bamboo basket, which can hold around fifty kilos of lightly packed leaf and is how the Wuzhou factories age and sell wholesale. From those baskets the tea is repacked into small baskets of a few hundred grams to a kilo, tins and boxes, or steamed again and pressed into bricks, cakes and small tuo for gifts. Baskets breathe and age the tea cleanly; bricks are slower and keep a piled note longer.

Grades run from Te Ji (special) through 1 to 6, and they are about leaf size and tenderness, not about quality of storage or age. A Te Ji is fine, even, mostly young leaf and brews smooth and refined; grade 3 is the everyday standard; grades 5 and 6 are coarse, stemmy and cheap, and they make a surprisingly sweet, rustic pot when simmered. In dark tea, stems are not a flaw: they add sweetness and are part of the style.

Two farmhouse products sit outside the grading. Lao Cha Po, 'old tea granny', is made from big, mature leaves picked in autumn and winter, best around and after Frost's Descent in late October, traditionally blanched in water, now more often steamed, then dried and stored. Growers kept it for their own drinking and as a home remedy. It looks like dried leaves off the forest floor and brews a light, honeyed, grain-like tea. Cha Guo (tea fruit) and tea flowers are sold the same way. Nong jia, farmhouse Liu Bao proper, is the unpiled, greener version of the main tea, which ages slowly along the lines of a raw pu-erh and tastes quite different from factory tea.

For brewing, graded leaf wants two rinses and boiling water in short steeps; coarse grades and Lao Cha Po are better simmered for five to ten minutes and kept warm. A brick or cake needs prying apart and a slightly longer rinse.

When buying, read the label for year, factory, batch and grade; pay for age and storage, not for a fancy basket; and try a cheap grade 5 or a Lao Cha Po before deciding Liu Bao is not for you, because the rustic end of the range is often the most charming.
history:
Grades are the formal side: Liu Bao is officially sorted into special grade and grades one to six, mostly by how tender the leaf is. Grade does not settle quality on its own, since this tea also changes with storage.

Lao Cha Po comes from the farmhouse side. Liubao growers once picked current-year or older mature leaves in autumn and winter, blanched them in water and later steamed them, then kept them for their own drinking and as home medicine. Leaf picked at or after Frost's Descent was the most prized. Little is documented about when each format began. Very large baskets remain in use: one 1999 lot, pressed in 2001, sold by the basket at about 50 kg.
